--- title: Exploring GoodReads Data author: Lucy Wright date: 2025-02-04 format: html: code-fold: true categories: [Python, 26Summer, "data: books.csv"] --- ![](bookpic.jpg) ## Set up We used Python and Quarto to investigate and present the GoodReads dataset. First we set up the environment. ::: {#58a0631f .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd import seaborn as sns import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import scipy.stats as stats ``` ::: ## Look at the data Then we wanted to know what the data set included by loading the data set, backing it up, and then viewing a small preview of the first two rows. ::: {#774fa817 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # load the data df_raw = pd.read_csv("../../../../data/books.csv") # back it up df = df_raw.copy() # display the first two rows df.head(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## How are are ratings spread over the 0-5 stars? ::: {#e3ab7d4c .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.relplot(df, x = "average_rating", y = "ratings_count") plt.xlabel("Average rating") plt.ylabel("Frequency") plt.show() # used this line to prevent a strange header that kept appearing ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](books_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=470 height=470} ::: ::: Did any books receive a rating of zero stars? ::: {#b40c2560 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} zerostars = df[df["average_rating"] == 0] zerostars.count() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` Unnamed: 0 26 bookID 26 title 26 authors 26 average_rating 26 isbn 26 isbn13 26 language_code 26 num_pages 26 ratings_count 26 text_reviews_count 26 publication_date 26 publisher 26 dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: Did any books not receive any ratings? ::: {#bfbb287a .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} zeroratings = df[df["ratings_count"] == 0] zeroratings.count() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` Unnamed: 0 81 bookID 81 title 81 authors 81 average_rating 81 isbn 81 isbn13 81 language_code 81 num_pages 81 ratings_count 81 text_reviews_count 81 publication_date 81 publisher 81 dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: Some books may have received an average_rating of zero stars, but it doesn't make sense that some books could have an average_rating without any ratings_count. Therefore we excluded data where the ratings_count was equal to or less than zero. ::: {#1ae6a127 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} df = df[df["ratings_count"] > 0] ``` ::: ***Look at that plot again*** Most people who read seem to think what they're reading is pretty good. ::: {#332e08da .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.relplot(df, x = "average_rating", y = "ratings_count") plt.xlabel("Average rating") plt.ylabel("Frequency") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](books_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){width=470 height=470} ::: ::: ## Are modern books better than older books or vice versa? First let's find out some basic information about this variable. What is the earliest publication date? ::: {#614779f7 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} df["publication_date"].min() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` '1900-01-01' ``` ::: ::: And the latest? ::: {#ba5abeac .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} df["publication_date"].max() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` '2020-03-31' ``` ::: ::: What does it look like on a scatterplot? ::: {#d58a8931 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.relplot(df, x = "publication_date", y = "average_rating", color = "pink") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](books_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.png){width=471 height=470} ::: ::: **SCARY!!!** Clean it up by excluding the month and day and only keeping the year. We needed to split the "publication_date" data to isolate the year. ::: {#c9f3537e .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} # Create a new object that splits the "publication_date" column by the "-" symbol. split_dates = df['publication_date'].str.split('-', expand=True) # We did some additional cleaning here to make sure we were dealing with ints and floats split_dates = split_dates.astype(int) ratings = df["average_rating"].astype(float) # Then add those split dates as new columns in our dataframe. df[["pub_year", "pub_month", "pub_day"]] = split_dates # try plot again sns.relplot(df, x = "pub_year", y = ratings, color = "pink") plt.xlabel("Publication year") plt.ylabel("Average rating") # We wanted a line of best fit so we tried sns.linplot # but quickly recognised that it wasn't what we were hoping for. sns.lineplot(df, x = "pub_year", y = ratings) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](books_files/figure-html/cell-12-output-1.png){width=470 height=470} ::: ::: This is nice but it would be better if the line was a regression line to show the trend and answer the question... # Stats Time! Here's a linear regression model plot. ::: {#ffd30737 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} lm = stats.linregress(x = df["pub_year"], y = ratings) # ask for a particular result print(lm.pvalue) # make a linear regression model plot sns.lmplot(data = df, x = "pub_year", y = "average_rating", line_kws={'color': 'red'}) plt.xlabel("Publication year") plt.ylabel("Average rating") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 9.045125408073782e-06 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](books_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-2.png){width=470 height=470} ::: ::: **Older books might be better than more modern books...** But it's possible this effect is being driven by outliers. So lets find out the mean year published, and the values 3SD above and below that date to exclude the outliers. The mean publication year is.... ::: {#ffd9af82 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} pubyear_mean = df["pub_year"].mean() print(round(pubyear_mean)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2000 ``` ::: ::: The standard deviation of pub_year is... ::: {#6b5e86d1 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} pubyear_std = df["pub_year"].std() print(round(pubyear_std)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 8 ``` ::: ::: So the window we could look at to exclude outliers is ::: {#9b6aab6d .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} # calculate the lower and upper limits lowerlimit = pubyear_mean - 3*pubyear_std upperlimit = pubyear_mean + 3*pubyear_std # apply this window to the pub_year column df = df[df["pub_year"] > lowerlimit] df = df[df["pub_year"] < upperlimit] ``` ::: Did the outcome change? The new p value is... ::: {#d4317ff6 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} lm = stats.linregress(x = df["pub_year"], y = df["ratings_count"]) # print the p value print(lm.pvalue) # make a linear regression model plot sns.lmplot(data = df, x = "pub_year", y = "average_rating", line_kws={'color': 'red'}) plt.xlabel("Publication year") plt.ylabel("Average rating") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 5.059499118535008e-06 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](books_files/figure-html/cell-17-output-2.png){width=470 height=470} ::: ::: It retains significance! Probably because there are so many data. But the graph is still pretty hard to read because of overplotting. Lets make it *pretty*. ::: {#cfe4ae4a .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} # make a linear regression model plot look *pretty* g = sns.lmplot( data = df, x = "pub_year", y = "average_rating", hue= "average_rating", palette = "viridis", fit_reg = False, legend = False, scatter_kws={"s": 5, 'alpha': 0.3}) #overlay a single global regression line sns.regplot(data = df, x = "pub_year", y = "average_rating", scatter = False, ax = g.axes[0,0], color = "black") # update axis labels plt.xlabel("Publication year") plt.ylabel("Average rating") # get the p value from before p_value = lm.pvalue # show the p value equation on the graph p_label = f'p = {p_value:.2e}' plt.legend(title='Regression Stats', labels=[p_label], loc='lower left') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](books_files/figure-html/cell-18-output-1.png){width=470 height=470} ::: :::
